back2basics.text: RPO is a regulatory mandate requiring electricity distribution companies and large consumers to source a specified minimum percentage of their electricity from renewable energy sources. It aims to promote clean energy adoption and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Compliance can be achieved by consuming renewable power, purchasing Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs), or paying a penalty if targets are unmet.

body.label: Phased RPO targets
body.text: KERC has set Renewable Procurement Obligation targets starting at 35.95% in 2026-27, increasing to 38.81% in 2027-28, 41.36% in 2028-29, and reaching 43.33% in 2029-30.

body.label: Entities covered
body.text: The targets apply to electricity distribution companies (Escoms) and obligated entities including open-access consumers with contracted demand of 1 MW or more, such as industries and commercial establishments.

sections.heading: What are the new renewable energy targets set by KERC?

body.label: Reducing coal dependence
body.text: Due to poor monsoon and shortages in hydropower and wind energy, Karnataka’s coal reliance has increased, prompting higher renewable targets to promote cleaner energy.

body.label: Alignment with national policy
body.text: KERC’s higher RPO targets align with the Union Ministry of New and Renewable Energy’s proposal to expand renewable obligations across stakeholders.

sections.heading: Why has KERC raised renewable energy targets?

body.label: Multiple compliance options
body.text: Entities can meet RPOs by consuming renewable electricity, purchasing Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs), or paying a buyout price if targets are unmet.

body.label: Monitoring and penalties
body.text: Entities must submit consumption details by July 31, 2027, with state agency monitoring and compliance reports due by August 31, 2027; non-compliance can lead to proceedings under Section 142 of the Electricity Act, 2003.

sections.heading: How will compliance with RPO targets be ensured?

body.label: Diverse renewable sources
body.text: The RPO covers solar, wind, hydropower, biomass, municipal solid waste-based energy, and distributed renewable energy such as rooftop solar and small projects below 10 MW.

body.label: New projects emphasized
body.text: Wind and hydropower RPOs must be met through projects commissioned after March 31, 2024, distinguishing newer renewable capacity from older installations.

back2basics.concept: UN Climate Change Conferences and Fossil Fuel Debate
back2basics.text: The UN Climate Change Conferences (COPs) are annual meetings where nearly 200 countries negotiate actions to address climate change. A key issue is how to handle fossil fuels, the main source of greenhouse gas emissions. Countries differ on explicitly naming fossil fuels in agreements due to economic and political interests. Achieving consensus is essential for global climate commitments but often challenging.

back2basics.concept: UN Climate Change Conferences and Consensus Decision-Making
back2basics.text: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) organizes annual Conferences of Parties (COP) where member countries negotiate climate action. Decisions require consensus, meaning all parties must agree, which can lead to stalemates if key countries disagree. These conferences aim to coordinate global efforts to limit climate change impacts.
